# Fire Water System Control Narrative: Fire Pumps FP-1, FP-2 and Jockey Pump JP-1

## 1. Corrections to the Client's Draft

Three items in the draft conflict with NFPA 20 and need to change before this narrative is issued.

| Client draft intent | Issue | Corrected intent |
|---|---|---|
| PLC starts fire pumps on low header pressure (PT-601) | NFPA 20 requires each listed fire pump controller to start its pump from its **own** pressure sensing line and transducer. A non-listed PLC and a shared transmitter would add a single point of failure to the start path. | Each listed controller starts its pump automatically from its own sensing line. The PLC **monitors only**. PT-601 is for indication, alarming and trending. It is not a start sensor. |
| PLC stops fire pumps after pressure recovers for 10 minutes | NFPA 20 allows stopping only (a) manually at the controller, or (b) automatically by the controller itself, if that feature is used and the AHJ accepts it. Automatic shutdown also requires the controller's minimum run timer: at least 10 min for electric and 30 min for diesel. A remote PLC stop is not permitted. | **Recommended:** manual stop only, at the controller, by an operator who has confirmed the fire is out. If the owner wants automatic shutdown, it must be configured inside the listed controller, with the minimum run timers above and AHJ/insurer approval. It is never done by the PLC. Most petrochemical owners and insurers require manual stop. |
| PLC trips FP-1 on low lube oil pressure and high coolant temperature | NFPA 20 allows a fire pump diesel engine to shut down automatically **only on overspeed**. Low oil pressure and high coolant temperature are **alarms only**. Running the engine to destruction during a fire is the intended design tradeoff. | No PLC trips of any kind. The engine's overspeed device (manual reset) is the only automatic shutdown. Low oil pressure and high coolant temperature are annunciated at the diesel controller and sent to the PLC as alarms. |

**General principle:** the PLC/SCADA has **no control authority** over FP-1 or FP-2. It must not:
- start or stop either pump,
- inhibit or delay a start,
- command or block the ATS,
- shed fire pump load, or
- act on the diesel fuel or cooling systems.

Loss of the PLC, its power, or its network must have zero effect on fire pump operation.

---

## 2. Scope and Responsibilities

| Function | Responsible device |
|---|---|
| Automatic start of FP-2 and FP-1 | Listed electric controller (FP-2) and listed diesel controller (FP-1), each on its own sensing line |
| Stop of FP-2 and FP-1 | Manual at the controller (recommended), or the controller's own automatic shutdown with minimum run timer if approved |
| Normal/emergency source transfer for FP-2 | Listed fire pump ATS, integral to the FP-2 controller assembly |
| Engine protection for FP-1 | Engine overspeed shutdown only. All other conditions alarm only. |
| Pressure maintenance | JP-1 controller (dedicated jockey controller with its own pressure sensing, recommended) |
| Supervisory signals required by code | Fire alarm control unit (FACU) per NFPA 72, to a constantly attended location |
| Monitoring, trending, operator alarms, test logging | Site PLC/SCADA (supplementary, non-required) |

**FACU vs. PLC.** NFPA 20 requires fire pump alarm and supervisory signals at a constantly attended location. These normally route through the listed FACU. The PLC can receive the same signals in parallel through separate dry contacts or an isolated interface. The PLC must not be the only path for any code-required signal unless the AHJ explicitly accepts it.

---

## 3. Setpoints

| Device | Start (psig) | Stop (psig) | Set in |
|---|---|---|---|
| JP-1 | 155 | 165 | JP-1 controller |
| FP-2 (electric, lead) | 145 | Manual (see §5.5) | FP-2 listed controller |
| FP-1 (diesel, lag) | 135 | Manual (see §5.5) | FP-1 listed controller |

**Review against NFPA 20 Annex guidance:**
- The jockey differential of 10 psi is acceptable.
- FP-2 starts 10 psi below the jockey start. The Annex guidance is 5 psi below, so 10 psi is acceptable and more conservative against nuisance starts.
- FP-1 starts 10 psi below FP-2, which matches the guidance for additional pumps.
- Electric lead / diesel lag is a reasonable arrangement. FP-1 still starts on its own pressure setpoint if FP-2 fails to start or loses power. No PLC logic is needed for backup start.

**Verify before final issue:**
1. **Jockey stop vs. churn.** Annex guidance sets jockey stop at fire pump churn pressure plus minimum static suction pressure. Get the certified pump curve and confirm 165 psig is consistent.
2. **System overpressure.** Check rated-pump churn (up to 140% of 150 psi = 210 psi) plus maximum suction pressure against component ratings, which are often 175 psi. For FP-1, NFPA 20 requires a pressure relief valve or listed variable speed pressure limiting control if 121% of net rated shutoff pressure plus maximum static suction pressure exceeds the system rating.
3. **Pressure maintenance during flowing.** Confirm JP-1 capacity is below the flow of the smallest single sprinkler/nozzle, so a real demand drops pressure to the fire pump start points.

---

## 4. Instrumentation

- **Controller sensing lines.** FP-1 and FP-2 each have an independent ½ in. sensing line. Each line taps between that pump's discharge check valve and discharge control valve and includes the code-required check/orifice arrangement. Do not tee the sensing lines together or share them with PT-601.
- **PT-601 (header pressure transmitter).** PLC indication, trending and alarms only. Mount it on its own tap.
- **Controller pressure recording.** Each listed controller records pressure and events internally. The PLC trend is supplementary.
- **LT-610 (diesel day/fuel tank level).** PLC indication and alarms. This does not replace the low-fuel signal from the FP-1 controller or tank switch, where the adopted NFPA 20 edition requires one.

---

## 5. Sequence of Operation

### 5.1 Normal Standby
- **FP-1 controller:**
  - in AUTO,
  - both battery sets charged,
  - engine jacket water heater energized,
  - fuel supply valve locked open.
- **FP-2 controller:**
  - in AUTO,
  - normal source available,
  - ATS on normal.
- **JP-1:** in AUTO, keeping the header at 155–165 psig.
- **PLC:**
  - displays status,
  - alarms any controller that is not in AUTO,
  - trends PT-601 and JP-1 run cycles.

### 5.2 Pressure Maintenance (JP-1)
1. Header pressure falls to 155 psig. The JP-1 controller starts JP-1.
2. Pressure rises to 165 psig. JP-1 stops. A minimum run timer in the JP-1 controller limits short-cycling.
3. PLC excessive-cycling alarm: more than X starts per hour, or run time over Y min per hour. This points to system leakage. The owner sets the thresholds.

### 5.3 Fire Demand: Lead Pump FP-2
1. Demand exceeds JP-1 capacity and pressure falls.
2. At 145 psig on FP-2's sensing line, the FP-2 controller starts FP-2.
3. If the normal source fails, the listed ATS transfers to the alternate source. This happens without PLC involvement.
4. PLC actions:
   - alarms "FP-2 Running",
   - logs the start time and PT-601 pressure,
   - notifies operators.

### 5.4 Fire Demand: Lag Pump FP-1
1. If pressure keeps falling, either because demand exceeds one pump or FP-2 failed to start, the FP-1 controller cranks FP-1 at 135 psig on its own sensing line.
2. The cranking cycle alternates between battery sets per NFPA 20: 6 cycles of 15 s crank / 15 s rest. If the engine still has not started, the controller annunciates crank failure.
3. The PLC alarms "FP-1 Running" or "FP-1 Fail to Start".

### 5.5 Stopping
- **Recommended:** both pumps keep running until an operator stops them manually at the controller, after the incident commander confirms the fire is out.
- **If automatic shutdown is approved:** it is set in the controller only. The minimum run time is 10 min for FP-2 and 30 min for FP-1. Shutdown happens only once pressure is restored and only for pressure-initiated starts. Pumps started manually or by a deluge/releasing input stop manually.
- **PLC:** no stop function, no remote stop pushbutton on SCADA, and no "pressure recovered" logic acting on the pumps.

### 5.6 Other Start Means (Optional)
- **Manual start:** at each controller. Remote manual start stations are allowed if they are wired directly to the controller as permitted by NFPA 20.
- **Deluge/water spray start:** a deluge valve or listed releasing panel may start the pumps through the controller's "start by other means" input. Use a listed fire alarm/releasing device, not the PLC. Pumps started this way stop manually.

### 5.7 Testing
- **FP-1:** weekly automatic no-flow test using the controller's weekly test timer, minimum 30 min (NFPA 25).
- **FP-2:** monthly no-flow test, minimum 10 min (current NFPA 25 editions). Confirm against the adopted edition and the owner's risk assessment, which may require weekly.
- **PLC:**
  - logs each test run (start, stop, duration, PT-601 suction/discharge if available),
  - flags missed tests.
  - Test starts come from the controller timer, not the PLC.

---

## 6. FP-1 Diesel Engine Protection

| Condition | Action |
|---|---|
| Overspeed | **Engine shutdown** by the engine's overspeed device. Manual reset at the controller is required. Alarm to the FACU and PLC. |
| Low lube oil pressure | **Alarm only.** The engine continues to run. |
| High coolant temperature | **Alarm only.** The engine continues to run. |
| Crank failure / fail to start | Alarm |
| Battery failure / charger failure (each set) | Alarm |
| ECM fault / fuel injection malfunction (electronic engines) | Alarm. Switching to the alternate ECM follows the engine listing. |
| Low fuel level | Alarm |
| Controller not in AUTO | Supervisory alarm |

The PLC receives these signals for display and alarming only. Operator response to low oil pressure or high temperature during a fire is the fire incident commander's decision, made locally at the controller.

---

## 7. PLC Monitoring Points (Inputs Only)

All signals are dry contacts from the listed controllers, or analog transmitters. The PLC has **no outputs** to FP-1, FP-2 or the FP-2 ATS.

| Tag | Description | Type | PLC alarm / action |
|---|---|---|---|
| FP1-RUN | FP-1 engine running | DI | Alarm "FP-1 Running". Log event. |
| FP1-FTS | FP-1 crank failure / fail to start | DI | High-priority alarm |
| FP1-TRBL | FP-1 engine trouble (common: low oil pressure, high coolant temp, overspeed, ECM fault) | DI | High-priority alarm. Break out individual points if the controller provides them. |
| FP1-AUTO | FP-1 controller not in AUTO | DI | Supervisory alarm |
| FP1-BATT | FP-1 battery/charger failure | DI | Alarm |
| FP2-RUN | FP-2 motor running | DI | Alarm "FP-2 Running". Log event. |
| FP2-FTS | FP-2 fail to start (where provided) | DI | High-priority alarm |
| FP2-PWR | FP-2 loss of power / phase failure / phase reversal | DI | High-priority alarm |
| FP2-ALT | FP-2 ATS on alternate source | DI | Alarm |
| FP2-TRBL | FP-2 controller trouble | DI | Alarm |
| JP1-RUN | JP-1 running | DI | Trend and cycle count. Excessive-cycling alarm. |
| PT-601 | Fire water header pressure | AI | Low alarm 150 psig (JP-1 not keeping up). Low-low 140 psig (fire pump demand). High alarm near system rating. Trend. |
| LT-610 | FP-1 fuel tank level | AI | Low alarm at ⅔ tank capacity or the level required by the adopted NFPA 20 edition. High alarm during filling. |
| TT-pump room | Pump room temperature | AI | Low alarm at ~72 °F for the diesel room (NFPA 20 minimum is 70 °F unless the engine manufacturer allows 40 °F with a jacket heater). ~45 °F where electric only. High alarm per engine manufacturer (typically 120 °F). |

**Sizing note:** NFPA 20 requires the fuel tank to hold at least 1 gal per engine hp, plus 5% for expansion and 5% for sump. Confirm that LT-610 alarm levels align with that capacity.

---

## 8. Failure Modes

| Failure | Effect on fire pumps |
|---|---|
| PLC failure / power loss / network loss | None. Controllers operate independently. Alarm to the FACU via the separate path. |
| PT-601 failure | None. PLC alarms instrument fault. |
| FP-2 fails to start or loses both sources | FP-1 starts at 135 psig on its own sensing line. |
| FP-1 fails to start | FP-2 continues (if running). Alarm. |
| JP-1 failure | Header decays to 145 psig and FP-2 starts. Excessive-start pattern alarms in the PLC. |

---

## 9. Items for Client Confirmation

1. The adopted NFPA 20 and NFPA 25 editions, the AHJ, and insurer (e.g., FM Global) requirements. Some insurers prohibit automatic shutdown entirely.
2. Manual-stop-only vs. controller-based automatic shutdown (recommended: manual).
3. Certified pump curves, so the jockey stop setpoint, churn pressure, overpressure and relief valve need can be checked.
4. The FACU interface for code-required supervisory signals, and whether the PLC is a parallel monitor only.
5. Whether deluge/water spray releasing panels will start the pumps directly, and confirmation that they are listed devices.
6. Signal availability from each controller model, to decide between individual alarms and common trouble.
